tip: Απαντάω σε (apandáo se) = reply to, and σε + το merge into στο (sto): απάντησα στο μήνυμά σου (apándisa sto mínimá su).
Πριν + στείλεις (prin stílis) = before you send – πριν normally takes the one-time verb form, not the ongoing one.
Τα ανεπιθύμητα (ta anepithímita) = the spam folder, literally the unwanted ones.
Γράψε μου (grápse mu) = text me, literally write to me.
No verb needed in the reply: εγώ τίποτα (egó típota) = me, nothing.
Έπεσε (épese) = it dropped – in Greek a connection falls rather than drops.
Κοντεύει να (kondévi na) is literally 'it nears to', from κοντά (kondá = near) – Greek's 'about to'. Κοντεύει να τελειώσει (kondévi na teliósi) = it's about to run out.
Πια (pia) = anymore or these days – it normally sits at the end of the sentence.
Άσε (áse), from αφήνω (afíno = to leave), builds 'let' commands with να (na): άσε το κινητό να φορτίσει (áse to kinitó na fortísi) = leave the phone to charge, i.e. let it charge.
Πολλή (polí) = much with a feminine noun: πολλή μνήμη (polí mními) – spelled with two λ, said with one.
Με τίποτα (me típota) = no matter what, literally with nothing.
Βάζω ξυπνητήρι (vázo ksipnitíri) = set an alarm, literally put an alarm.
Στο αθόρυβο (sto athórivo) = on silent, literally in the noiseless.
Lights in Greek are normally lit, not switched: άναψε (ánapse) comes from ανάβω (anávo = light, ignite), the verb for a φακός (fakós = flashlight), lamps and fires alike.
Είπαμε (ípame) = we agreed, literally we said – it holds someone to a deal.
Ξέρω από (kséro apó) is literally I know from, and it means being good with something: δεν ξέρει από τεχνολογία (dhen kséri apó tekhnoloyía) = he's no good with technology.
Instructions normally use the present: πατάς εδώ και ανοίγει (patás edhó ke aníyi) = you tap here and it opens.
Plural καλημέρες (kaliméres) = good-morning images – a whole genre.
'Everything that' is όλα όσα (óla ósa) – literally 'all as-many-as'. The English instinct όλα που (óla pu) sounds off: quantities take όσα (ósa), not που (pu).
Κόλλησε (kólise) = it froze, literally it got stuck.
Άνοιξέ το (ánikse to) = open it – the command picks up a second accent because το follows it.
Ζεσταίνεται (zesténete) = it gets hot – the -εται (-ete) ending points the action back at the thing itself.
Greek takes a photo out: βγάζεις μια φωτογραφία (vgházis mia fotoghrafía) uses βγάζω (vgházo = take out), not παίρνω (pérno = take).
After feeling verbs the 'that' is που (pu), not ότι (óti): χαίρομαι που σε βλέπω (khérome pu se vlépo) = I'm glad that I see you. Joy, sadness and anger all take που.
Μαζευόμαστε (mazevómaste) = we gather – the -όμαστε (-ómaste) ending turns the action back on us.
Γυρίζω σπίτι (yirízo spíti) = I come home – no στο (sto) needed before σπίτι.
Με στενοχώρησε (me stenokhórise) = it upset me, the thing acting on you – flip it with στενοχωριέμαι (stenokhoriéme) = I get upset. Same verb, other direction.
Βαριέμαι (variéme) = I'm bored has no plain-verb form, only the -μαι (-me) one. Greek feeling verbs often look like this: κοιμάμαι (kimáme = I sleep), φοβάμαι (fováme = I fear).
Βαριέμαι (variéme) alone = I'm bored. Add να (na) + a verb and it shifts: βαριέμαι να μαγειρεύω (variéme na mayirévo) = I can't be bothered to cook.
Θυμώνω με (thimóno me) = get angry at – Greek uses με (me), literally with.
